item.title: PostgreSQL JSON Indexing Strategies for Array Containment Queries
item.description:
“PostgreSQL JSON Indexing Strategies for Array Containment Queries”

How can database architects effectively index columns storing JSON data, specifically arrays, within PostgreSQL to accelerate containment searches, especially when dealing with versions prior to 9.4 or when seeking specialized performance characteristics?

The introduction of the binary JSON data type, jsonb, in PostgreSQL 9.4 significantly expanded indexing capabilities for semi-structured data. When dealing with JSON arrays embedded within a column, standard B-tree indexes offer little benefit for deep containment checks. The solution revolves around specialized index types, namely GIN (Generalized Inverted Index), and leveraging appropriate operators.

item.title: MySQL Max Key Length Error: Strategies for 'Specified key was too long'
item.description:
“MySQL Max Key Length Error: Strategies for ‘Specified key was too long’”

This persistent error message, “Specified key was too long; max key length is 767 bytes,” typically arises when you attempt to create an index, particularly a unique index, on a VARCHAR or CHAR column in MySQL, and the combined length of the indexed columns, considering their character encoding, exceeds the maximum allowed prefix length for an index.

The primary culprit is often the character encoding used. MySQL’s utf8mb4 encoding, which supports a wider range of characters including emojis, uses up to 4 bytes per character. This significantly impacts how many characters can fit within the 767-byte limit. For utf8 encoding, which uses up to 3 bytes per character, the limit translates to roughly 255 characters.
